name: Kaan Aksit
summary: This project focuses on merging artificial intelligence techniques with physical principles to enhance the realism of immersive displays. Situated at the intersection of AI, physics, and display technology, the research aims to develop innovative solutions for tasks such as realistic rendering, haptic feedback, or motion tracking within virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) contexts. Students will leverage high-performance computing, optimization algorithms, and machine learning techniques to design and implement physically informed AI algorithms. The work involves exploring how physical principles can inform and enhance AI models, providing hands-on experience with state-of-the-art hardware and software tools. This interdisciplinary project is suitable for students in UCL's Master's program in Scientific and Data Intensive Computing who are interested in the integration of physics and AI. Participants will develop valuable skills in data analysis, optimization, and high-performance computing while contributing to groundbreaking research in immersive technologies. The project offers an opportunity to work within a dynamic environment alongside researchers and industry professionals.

name: Timo Betcke
summary: This project focuses on addressing the current lack of robust GPU acceleration support within the Rust programming language, which is an increasingly popular choice for scientific computing. The primary objective is to investigate existing GPU computing toolkits available for Rust and explore ways to evolve the language's GPU computing ecosystem. To achieve this, the student will set up benchmark experiments to evaluate these tools. The work is experimental and software-oriented, involving the investigation of toolkit capabilities and performance benchmarking. This project is ideal for students interested in systems programming, scientific computing, and the development of high-performance computing ecosystems. While no specific technical prerequisites are listed, applicants should be prepared to dedicate substantial time to the project throughout the entire academic year. The research aims to bridge the gap between Rust's growing popularity in scientific domains and its current limitations regarding hardware acceleration.

name: Nikos Nikolaou
summary: Supervisor Nikos Nikolaou offers two distinct experimental research projects focusing on different dimensions of deep learning. The first project investigates uncertainty estimation and interpretability in machine learning models applied to medical imaging tasks, aiming to evaluate how improved uncertainty quantification affects model trustworthiness and identifies prediction failures or biases. Students will work with real-world imaging data, handling challenges like class imbalance and image alignment using architectures such as CNNs or ViTs. Alternatively, the second project explores alternative training paradigms that move beyond backpropagation limitations, specifically investigating local learning rules, Hebbian updates, and the NoProp framework to address biological implausibility and high memory usage. This implementation-focused work involves benchmarking methods on image classification and sequence modeling while exploring intersections with network sparsity and pruning strategies. The medical imaging project is suitable for students interested in uncertainty or interpretability, requiring Python proficiency and experience with imaging applications. The second project requires a strong mathematical and algorithmic background, ideal for those interested in biologically inspired learning mechanisms and efficient model training.

name: Guido Germano
summary: This software-oriented project aims to improve the performance of QMGA, an open-source C++ molecular graphics program used for the interactive, rendered representation of large ensembles of convex bodies in coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations. The primary scientific objective is to enhance rendering speed and accessibility for datasets that now reach millions of particles. Students can choose between two main development paths. One option focuses on modernizing the existing OpenGL-based C++ codebase by updating library calls and makefiles for Linux, moving the distribution to GitHub, and implementing recent OpenGL developments like occlusion queries, backface culling, and vertex buffer objects, potentially porting the result to macOS and Windows. Alternatively, a second path involves rewriting the program using WebGL and JavaScript to create 'WebMGA,' a version designed for universal compatibility without complex builds or library dependencies. The project is highly coding-heavy and suitable for students interested in computer graphics, high-performance software engineering, and web-based visualization technologies.

name: Mose Giordano
summary: This software-oriented project focuses on developing a high-performance implementation of an algorithm based on the non-equispaced fast Fourier transform for the Lomb-Scargle.jl package in Julia. The scientific context involves Astronomy, specifically using the Lomb-Scargle periodogram to detect periods in periodic, potentially unevenly sampled signals such as variable star light curves. The primary objective is to write this new implementation and conduct a performance comparison against existing algorithms within the LombScargle.jl open-source package. The work is highly coding-intensive, requiring the student to contribute directly to a scientific computing library using the Julia programming language. While specific student interests are not explicitly listed, the project involves implementing complex algorithms and evaluating computational efficiency. The task is centered on algorithmic development and performance optimization within the existing framework of the LombScargle.jl repository.

name: Peter Bentley
summary: These projects explore the intersection of generative deep learning and evolutionary computation to advance automated optimization and design. One project aims to develop a distributed generative design process mimicking biological development, using cellular automata or multi-agent systems alongside GANs or VAEs to create complex 3D geometries where form fits function. This coding-heavy, experimental task involves using genetic algorithms or novelty search to enable adaptive growth in response to environmental constraints. A second project investigates improving optimization and exploration by learning latent representations from existing solutions via GANs or VAEs. The student will compare how different generative approaches handle multiobjective or constrained optimization, specifically examining the precise representations of GANs against the fuzzy encoder-decoder structure of VAEs. Research involves testing if these learned spaces can effectively map evolved latent variables back to a phenotype for real-world problems. These projects are suitable for students interested in advanced representation learning and automated optimization; essential prerequisites include Python programming and experience with machine learning or evolutionary computation.

name: Edina Rosta
summary: Edina Rosta offers several distinct research projects spanning molecular dynamics, protein science, and causal inference. One project focuses on applying autoencoders to identify latent space for protein dynamics, while another develops Machine Learning Transition State Analysis (MLTSA) using neural networks and Gradient Boosting Decision Trees for drug design. A third option advances a reinforcement learning framework for autonomous bias placement in simulations using PPO or SAC agents, alongside a project exploring biased sampling on kinetic networks via stochastic block models and kinetic Monte Carlo algorithms. Additionally, students can investigate NTP-processing enzyme classification by integrating protein language models and AlphaFold to predict Enzyme Commission numbers. Another research direction applies causal discovery algorithms, such as PCMCI and Transfer Entropy, to identify directional relationships in molecular trajectories. These projects are computationally oriented, requiring proficiency in Python, Linux, and statistics, with specific needs for tools like PyTorch, OpenMM, or Matlab. Ideal candidates possess interests in structural enzymology, mechanistic modeling, or complex system dynamics, and backgrounds in Biophysics or Computational Chemistry are encouraged.

name: Kris Thielemans
summary: Kris Thielemans offers three distinct research projects focused on improving quantitative accuracy in molecular imaging. The first project, 'Partial Volume Correction in PET Imaging of the Lung', involves adapting PVE correction techniques to thoracic challenges like air content using Python and SIRF software through image simulation and potential 3D printed object scanning. The second project explores using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to estimate average PET sensitivity for motion correction, aiming to reduce computational expense during reconstruction. A third project focuses on improving PET accuracy by evaluating energy-based scatter correction methods, utilizing STIR software to compare PDF calculation approaches like the Method of Moments against Single Scatter Simulation. Additionally, one research opportunity aims to use machine learning techniques, such as 3D U-Net or Swin UNETR, to denoise SPECT images for better quantification in small volumes. These projects range from experimental and coding-heavy tasks to data-driven investigations involving Monte Carlo simulations. Essential prerequisites include programming experience in Python, MATLAB, or C++, with some projects requiring a basic understanding of machine learning or CNN architectures.

name: Michael Parkes
summary: This software-oriented project aims to develop a programme for analysing 3D Background Orientated Schlieren (BOS) images to examine density changes in materials. The primary objective is to create code capable of processing various image formats, including JPEG, TIF, and PNG, as well as movie frames like MPEG and AVI, applying the BOS method to identify chemical and physical changes. A key component involves processing images from a plenoptic camera by setting different depths of field and focal points to produce 3D understandings of density variations. The student will implement features to generate BOS images and velocity fields, alongside generating BOS backgrounds using methods such as wavelet or Pellin noise. This work involves handling large numbers of files and performing complicated analysis procedures to achieve 3D imaging capabilities. The project is highly coding-heavy, focusing on computational processing to detect minute differences between images. It provides an opportunity to apply computational techniques to scientific problems, such as studying concentration gradients in mixing fluids like water and alcohol.

name: Gopinathan Sankar
summary: This project focuses on the analysis of data derived from Synchrotron Radiation based X-ray techniques. The primary objective involves developing or applying methods to interpret complex datasets produced by these advanced X-ray technologies. Given the nature of the work, the project is centered around data analysis within the scientific context of synchrotron radiation research. Students will engage in investigating and processing experimental outputs to extract meaningful physical or chemical insights from the X-ray measurements. The work is fundamentally data-driven, requiring a focus on handling specialized datasets generated by high-intensity light sources. While specific programming languages or mathematical prerequisites are not explicitly detailed, the project necessitates an interest in advanced analytical techniques and the application of computational methods to experimental physics or materials science data. This research opportunity is ideal for students interested in the intersection of large-scale scientific facilities and sophisticated data processing workflows.

name: Ben Waugh
summary: Ben Waugh supervises three distinct software and research projects within particle physics. The first project focuses on refactoring the Atlantis Java application, an event display for LHC proton collisions, to improve its testability, maintainability, and extensibility; this requires knowledge of object-oriented design, with experience in Java and design patterns being advantageous. The second project involves enhancing the YODA C++ library by introducing full chi-squared support using the Eigen library and modernising its interface with the Contur tool to better handle uncertainty information. This software-oriented task is ideal for students interested in scientific software and high-performance C++ development. The third project investigates applying machine learning techniques, such as active learning, to the Python-based Contur toolkit to more efficiently test Beyond the Standard Model theories against LHC data. This research-driven project explores using ML to optimize parameter scanning, find best-fit values, or search for anomalies in measurements. These projects are suited for students interested in scientific computing, applied statistics, and real-world physics applications.

name: Frank Smith
summary: This project involves investigating fluid flows through a branching vessel to determine how much throughput is possible as the number of branches increases. The research will be conducted in two spatial dimensions, at least during the initial stages, focusing on high flow rates. The investigation will employ a combination of modelling, analysis, and computation to address the core research question. While the background motivation for this work is biomedical, the study also has relevance to several industrial applications. Students can expect a project that integrates mathematical modelling with computational techniques to explore fluid dynamics in complex structures. The work requires an approach capable of handling both analytical and numerical aspects of flow through branching networks. This project is suitable for students interested in fluid mechanics, computational modelling, and the intersection of biomedical and industrial engineering problems.

name: Anthony Lynas-Gray
summary: This supervisor offers two distinct computational projects in astrophysics. The first project focuses on time-frequency analysis of an interrupted light curve, specifically implementing the method of Jorge et al. (2006) into a computer program to analyse photometry of V2076 Oph. This work addresses limitations in Fourier transforms when dealing with non-sinusoidal or time-dependent variations in variable star brightness. The second project investigates the potential for a new determination of the Gravitational Constant (G) using light deflections by Solar System objects. Centred on the context of the Square Kilometre Array, this software-oriented task involves writing a program to reproduce Li et al. (2022) predictions for maximum gravitational deflection and calculating appropriate error bars. The student will then assess the prospects for determining G by comparing measured and observed deflections of light from objects outside the Solar System. Both projects involve significant programming and data analysis, targeting students interested in implementing complex mathematical models and evaluating fundamental physical constants through computational methods.

name: Gabriel Facini
summary: This supervisor offers two distinct research opportunities at the interface of AI and experimental particle physics within the UCL ATLAS group. The first project focuses on applying transformer architectures to Higgs boson tagging at the energy frontier, specifically identifying Higgs bosons decaying into two b-quarks in extreme kinematic regimes. This work involves developing models, addressing explainability through XAI methods to ensure interpretability, and evaluating performance on ATLAS Run 3 collision data using Python and ATLAS software frameworks. The second project explores Large Language Models (LLMs) to improve access to distributed scientific knowledge within the ATLAS collaboration. Students may fine-tune LLMs, implement advanced Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) techniques, or explore GraphRAG to develop a custom chatbot for querying documentation and resources. This project is highly software-oriented, involving natural language processing and large-scale data systems. While no explicit prerequisites are listed, the work requires a willingness to work independently and an interest in deep learning, machine learning, or big data applications within fundamental physics.

name: Kjell Erlandsson
summary: This project focuses on addressing the impact of patient motion in dynamic Positron Emission Tomography (PET) by investigating the use of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to correct parametric images. In dynamic PET, radiotracer distribution is measured over time and analyzed via kinetic modelling to produce parametric images; however, unavoidable motion during long scans can significantly degrade these results. The research objective is to explore a novel approach using deep learning for motion correction, which differs from traditional blind deconvolution methods used for blurring removal. This work presents an opportunity for potential publication through its innovative methodology. Students will investigate and implement CNN architectures to achieve effective motion correction in the context of parametric imaging. Essential prerequisites include programming experience, ideally in Python or MATLAB. While not strictly required, a basic knowledge of CNN architectures for imaging and training is desired. The project is well-suited for students with an interest in making meaningful contributions to research through deep learning applications in medical imaging.

name: Mark Buitelaar
summary: This project aims to develop machine learning algorithms to automate the tuning of carbon nanotube double quantum dot devices, which serve as essential building blocks for solid-state charge or spin qubits. As large-scale devices require numerous gate electrodes, manual tuning becomes a formidable task; this research intends to use machine learning techniques to address this challenge. The student will develop and test algorithms using data acquired from ultraclean carbon nanotube double quantum dot devices measured in a mK dilution refrigerator via radio-frequency reflectometry readout. Because data acquisition has been optimized for video-mode speed, large datasets are available for analysis. The project involves a trial-and-error approach as machine learning is a new development in the lab. Ideal candidates should possess a strong interest in quantum physics, solid-state physics, and computer science, and essential experience with machine learning techniques is required. This work combines experimental data acquisition with algorithmic development to optimize the control of quantum dot qubits.

name: Michel Tsamados
summary: This project focuses on expanding the capabilities of the ARISGAN software, which was previously developed to super-resolve OLCI optical imagery from Sentinel-3 to the higher resolution of Sentinel-2. The main objective is to adapt this Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) approach to achieve 5x super-resolution of microwave imager data from Sentinel-1 (50m resolution) to the Sentinel-2 resolution. The research is situated within the domain of Arctic sea ice monitoring, specifically aiming to synthesize artificial 'daylight' imagery at super-resolution during nighttime or cloudy conditions when the Sentinel-1 microwave sensor can still penetrate surface obstructions. The student will build upon existing software to implement and test this new super-resolution approach for microwave frequencies. This work is highly data-driven and involves working with multi-spectral satellite imagery. The project offers an opportunity to contribute to practical applications, such as providing satellite information to Inuit social enterprises in Pond Inlet to ensure safe ice travel. The task requires adapting complex deep learning models to different sensor types and resolutions.

name: Marta Betcke
summary: Marta Betcke offers several distinct research opportunities focusing on the intersection of machine learning and computational physics. One project explores learning correction for long steps in pseudo-spectral methods for solving the wave equation, while another investigates learned parallel in-time integration of dynamical systems. Research into neural operators is available for solving oscillatory problems such as the Helmholtz, Wave, and Westervelt equations. Other topics include using weakly convex neural networks for inverse problem regularisation and employing diffusion models as priors for inverse problem solutions. For those interested in medical imaging, one project focuses on photoacoustic image reconstruction methods—potentially involving learning optimal acquisition protocols or time-dependent regularisers—while another involves developing an image reconstruction platform for ultrasound tomography through research software engineering to handle diverse scanners and solvers. These projects range from theoretical and method-driven investigations to software-oriented development tasks. Interested students should contact the supervisor for specific details regarding each project's requirements.

name: Franca Fraternali
summary: Two distinct computational projects are available under the supervision of Franca Fraternali. The first project focuses on protein engineering using Transformer-based models to perform in-silico sequence evolution across various protein families and domains. The student will investigate potential model biases by running these architectures, exploring generated sequences, and using libraries like NumPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib to analyze changes in model embeddings. This data-driven project requires strong Python programming skills and knowledge of Machine Learning. The second project addresses hit-to-lead drug discovery by integrating Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations with Machine Learning to optimize chemical structures. The objective is to combine the accuracy of MD-based free energy methods, such as Free Energy Perturbation, with the efficiency of ML-based compound selection. The student will perform MD simulations and estimate binding free energies for compounds selected via embedding similarity, involving light coding for simulation management and result analysis. Both projects are computationally oriented, focusing on leveraging advanced algorithmic frameworks to improve predictive accuracy and screening efficiency in bioinformatics and drug development.

name: Jamie Dean
summary: This project addresses the challenge of reducing neurocognitive side effects in paediatric central nervous system tumours by investigating how different brain regions respond to radiotherapy. Using a dataset from mice treated with proton beam radiotherapy, the research aims to identify radiation-sensitive brain regions and the underlying molecular mechanisms. The work involves multimodal data integration, mapping radiotherapy dose maps, digital histology images, and molecular sequencing data onto a shared spatial coordinate system defined by a brain atlas. Students will implement state-of-the-art machine learning models for cell segmentation and identity labelling, while also measuring changes in cell type abundance and shape across different regions. Additionally, the project requires performing statistical analyses to identify molecular differences in cellular responses to radiation. This is a data-driven, interdisciplinary project involving the application of machine learning and statistical analysis to a high-priority biomedical problem. No prior knowledge of biology or medicine is necessary, making it suitable for students interested in large-scale biological data integration and advanced computational modeling.

name: Nora Yitong Qiu
summary: Nora Yitong Qiu offers two distinct research opportunities. The first project focuses on improving Optical Character Recognition (OCR) accuracy for premodern East Asian scripts, such as Manchu documents and Chinese calligraphy, by developing and applying AI and machine learning techniques. Students may train models on annotated corpora to address challenges like brushwork variability and archival degradation, making this suitable for those with technical backgrounds or interests in digital humanities, historical linguistics, and archival accessibility. The second project utilizes the China Biographical Database (CBDB) to conduct a social network analysis of elite political networks in imperial China. Using sociological methods, including regression modeling and longue durée historical comparison, students will investigate how kinship, patronage, and examination ties shaped bureaucratic hierarchies and influenced imperial power across different dynasties like the Tang, Yuan, or Qing. This research explores themes of ethnicity, alliance-building, and the evolution of oligarchic or meritocratic structures. Both projects provide opportunities for data-driven investigation into historical Chinese contexts through either computational modeling or sociological analysis.

name: Adam Gibson
summary: This project aims to develop a data-driven, AI-assisted system to automate the collation of early modern printed books, addressing the slow and error-prone nature of traditional manual text comparison. Working with a large dataset of digitized pages, the research focuses on identifying subtle textual variations caused by stop-press corrections. You will develop algorithms for preprocessing images, registration, detecting variants, and classifying them into types, while also considering user interface design for scholars. Technical challenges include handling page curvature, warping, bleed-through, and image alignment across different digitization systems, alongside exploring alternatives to OCR like pixel-based comparison on a coordinate grid. The work may involve supervised learning with labelled examples or unsupervised clustering of page states. This open-ended project is suitable for students interested in problem-solving and applying AI to historical or cultural data. The implementation will require distinguishing printed text from annotations and artefacts to create a successful proof-of-concept that improves the speed and accuracy of textual collation in digital humanities.

name: Jon Butterworth
summary: This software-oriented project aims to optimise the Contur toolkit, a Python-based tool used in particle physics to test Beyond the Standard Model (BSM) theories against CERN Large Hadron Collider data. Testing these theories is computationally expensive because it requires generating predictions across large parameter spaces to identify compatible regions. While a database design and basic interactive interface already exist for storing relational information between models, grids, and histograms, the current analysis process is time-consuming and resource-intensive. The student will focus on improving performance by benchmarking and profiling Python code, analysing database queries, and implementing and testing techniques to optimise both the code and the database. This work is highly technical and involves investigating ways to obtain results more quickly and explore them more effectively. To succeed, students should have familiarity with the UNIX shell, Python, SQL and database technologies, and git. The project is ideal for those interested in computational physics, software optimisation, and database performance enhancement.

name: Maxim Molodsov
summary: This project investigates the fundamental biological problem of how cells achieve extreme DNA compaction while maintaining accessibility for reading, copying, and repairing genes. The research focuses on understanding the integration of two distinct organizational mechanisms: liquid-like condensates formed by multivalent interactions between nucleosomes, and loop extrusion driven by the molecular machine condensin. Using the LAMMPS molecular dynamics simulator, the student will test how these two mechanisms work together mechanistically. This computational project is suited for a student with a strong interest in biology and good modelling experience. The work involves investigating the interplay between nucleosome-based interactions and active DNA looping to clarify how genome organization is maintained. By employing molecular dynamics simulations, the project provides an opportunity to explore the physical principles of genomic architecture through a modeling-heavy approach.

name: Jonathan Tennyson
summary: Supervisor Jonathan Tennyson offers four distinct research opportunities. One project involves constructing a new database of cooling functions for the ExoMol website, utilizing existing data to model processes ranging from the early universe to planetary atmospheres. Another software-oriented project focuses on expanding the ExoAtoms database by capturing and formatting external data on highly charged atoms into standard ExoMol format; students may find the Information Retrieval and Data Mining course helpful. A third project is a data-driven investigation into determining the approximate ages of exoplanets by matching planets from known catalogues with available host star age data. Finally, a workflow-oriented project aims to automate the MARVEL procedure—used for determining accurate molecular energy levels—by building a complete pipeline that utilizes data provided by large language models. These projects range from database construction and data formatting to algorithmic automation and astronomical data matching, catering to students interested in computational chemistry, astroinformatics, or automated scientific workflows.

name: Nikos Konstantinidis
summary: This project investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably assess MSci/MSc project reports when provided with an explicit marking rubric and assessment criteria. The research focuses on comparing the grades and criterion-level judgments produced by several publicly accessible LLMs against those assigned by human academic markers. Using a corpus of previously graded reports, the study will quantify the level of agreement between models and humans to identify which models align most closely with professional judgment. Additionally, the work will test whether LLM outputs can enhance inter-marker consistency through rubric-based calibration or function as an effective third cross-check during human marker disagreements. This data-driven investigation involves analyzing model performance and evaluating the utility of LLMs in academic assessment workflows. The project is centered on the intersection of natural language processing and educational assessment, specifically focusing on the reliability and practical application of automated grading tools.

name: William Woof
summary: Two distinct research projects are available focusing on deep learning applications in ophthalmology. The first project, 'Vision-language fusion for rare eye diseases', addresses the limitation of small datasets in diagnosing rare eye diseases by investigating how foundation language and vision-language models can bootstrap data through natural language instructions from experts. This pilot study focuses on using off-the-shelf models with small-scale fine-tuning rather than training new models from scratch. The second project, 'EyeNomaly', explores anomaly detection for Inherited Retinal Dystrophies (IRDs). Building upon the Eye2Gene classifier and existing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) used to generate retinal scans, this work investigates adapting trained GANs to flag potential eye disorders by identifying anomalies in patient data. This project is particularly suited for students interested in deep unsupervised learning. Both projects operate within the domain of medical imaging and deep learning, offering opportunities to work with generative models, vision-language fusion, and automated disease identification.

name: Tony Lynas-Gray
summary: Supervisor Tony Lynas-Gray offers three distinct computational projects. The first focuses on software development, requiring students to set up the NEMESISPY retrieval code and write a program to generate opacity tables for specific molecules using ExoMol database data. The second project is more algorithmic, involving writing programs to calculate opacity distribution functions (ODF) from monochromatic opacities and implementing one-dimensional radiative transfer to optimize bin-size. The third project is a physics-oriented programming task centered on General Relativity; students will develop a program to calculate the necessary time corrections for lunar surface observations relative to the Solar System Barycentre. All three projects are coding-heavy and involve computational modeling. Prerequisites include specific scientific readings, such as Yang et al. (2024) or Ashby & Patla (2024), and the High Performance Computing (PHAS0102) module is recommended for all options. These projects are ideal for students interested in molecular spectroscopy, planetary atmospheres, or relativistic astrophysics, but they are not suited for those seeking purely experimental or observational laboratory work.

name: Sergey Yurchenko
summary: This software-oriented project aims to address the computational bottleneck in exoplanet atmospheric modelling by developing the ExoMol Opacity App. While the ExoMol project provides essential high-temperature molecular data for interpreting observations from missions like the James Webb Space Telescope and ESA Ariel, current pre-computed opacity tables lack the flexibility to capture the diversity of newly discovered exoplanets. The student will design and implement a web interface that enables atmospheric modellers to configure custom opacity requests by selecting specific spectral ranges, resolutions, temperatures, pressures, and compositions. This work involves building a system capable of submitting these requests to high-performance computing (HPC) resources and retrieving tailored results. Consequently, the project combines web development, HPC job scheduling, and large-scale data handling. The implementation will directly empower the global astronomy community by allowing for customized atmospheric retrievals. This project is ideal for students interested in developing functional tools that bridge web technologies with complex scientific computing and large-scale data management.

name: Federico Galvanin
summary: This project aims to develop a digital twin for liquid-liquid extraction (LLE) systems used in the recovery of precious metals within continuous flow small channels. The research focuses on modeling segmented flow, where two immiscible liquids create patterns of slugs and plugs, to determine mass transfer rates between phases. The student will implement a joint system identification framework that utilizes model-based design of experiments (MBDoE) and active learning to develop a hybrid model. This approach involves combining data-driven modeling for hydrodynamics with first-principles modeling for mass transfer. The resulting digital twin will be used for LLE process simulation and scenario-based optimization. The work is interdisciplinary, blending machine learning counterparts like active learning with physics-based modeling and chemical engineering principles. Students interested in hybrid modeling, system identification, and the application of digital technologies to accelerate chemical process development will find this project suitable. The project focuses on the intersection of mathematical modeling, data-driven approaches, and fluid dynamics in small-scale extraction systems.

name: Siyin Liu
summary: This project addresses the challenge of manual, subjective analysis in corneal disease monitoring by developing an AI-powered pipeline for automated, quantitative In-Vivo Confocal Microscopy (IVCM) image analysis. Using Fuchs Endothelial Corneal Dystrophy (FECD) as a primary disease model, the research aims to discover novel digital biomarkers to identify subtle cellular changes during the disease's preclinical phase. Leveraging a unique longitudinal dataset from the FECD-TRACE cohort, the student will design, train, and validate an end-to-end deep learning pipeline. The work involves tackling various computer vision challenges, such as developing robust classifiers for image quality control, building segmentation models for quantifying cellular pathology, or exploring self-supervised learning with Vision Transformers like DINO for representation learning. This data-driven project requires the student to perform data pre-processing, model training, tuning, and rigorous validation. The specific focus can be tailored to the student's interests within the scope of these deep learning tasks, making it suitable for those interested in applying advanced computer vision techniques to clinical imaging and the discovery of unbiased biomarkers.
